playbook:
# Estate Game Playbook

When I land on an unowned property in early laps (laps 1-2), I will buy it if I have at least 80-100 cash remaining after purchase. Property ownership generates ongoing rent income and counts toward final score, making early acquisitions valuable.

When I land on an unowned property in mid laps (laps 3-4), I will buy if I have cash reserves of at least 60 after purchase. Mid-game is critical for acquiring remaining deeds before the board fills up. A balance of 60+ is sufficient to absorb one or two rent hits while still holding deeds for final scoring.

When I land on an unowned property in late laps (lap 5+), I will not buy. By this point, there are too few turns remaining for new properties to generate rent income, and my cash on hand counts directly toward final score. Only pass-throughs of START matter.

When I land on an owned property and owe rent, I will pay immediately and declare my reduced balance accurately.

When I land on a property I own, I will do nothing—no payment is owed.

When I pass START, I will collect my salary and add it to my balance.

When deciding whether to buy a property, I will not overextend myself early just to acquire deeds. The game rewards both deed value AND cash on hand. A low cash position leaves me vulnerable to unexpected rent demands.

I will track the property holdings of other players so I can anticipate which properties are still available and which rent obligations might come my way.

I will maintain a working cash reserve rather than depleting myself to own multiple properties early. However, I should be more aggressive in mid-game (laps 3-4) when opportunity presents itself, rather than passing on buys out of excessive caution.

I will aim to own 2-3 properties by the end of lap 4. This balances deed value with sufficient cash reserves to survive rent payments through lap 6.

In my last game I finished with 103 cash + 2 deeds (Quarry 60 + Depot 50) = 213, but scored 223. This suggests I missed rent income or miscalculated. I should have been more aggressive buying Terrace in lap 3 instead of passing.

# Playbook for ref_estate__shipped

When I land on an unowned property, I will buy it if I can afford it while maintaining at least 10-15 cash as a buffer. Owning properties is essential for generating income from other players and blocking competitors from acquiring valuable tiles.

When I land on a property owned by another investor, I will pay the rent without negotiation and track my cash carefully to avoid insolvency.

When I pass START, I will immediately add the salary to my running cash total before making any purchase decisions on that turn.

When deciding whether to buy a property, I will consider:
- The purchase price relative to my current cash
- Whether I can maintain a minimum cash reserve after purchase
- How many laps remain (buying early and mid-game is generally better than buying late)
- The property's rental income potential relative to its cost

I will keep meticulous records of my cash balance after every transaction, declared to the bank, so I know exactly what I have available.

When I own a property and land on it, I will pay nothing and declare my current balance unchanged (except for any salary collected or payments received that turn).

I will not attempt to speculate on which properties will be most profitable. Instead, I will acquire available properties systematically whenever I have sufficient cash, prioritizing acquisition volume over selectivity.

My goal is to maximize my final score: declared cash plus the purchase price of all deeds I hold. This means I should end the game with modest cash reserves and a diversified portfolio of properties, not with large cash hoards.

I should buy properties aggressively in laps 1-4 to maximize the time those properties generate rent. By lap 4, I should have a significant portfolio in place.

In lap 5 and especially lap 6, I should be very conservative about new purchases since there is minimal time for those purchases to generate return. Late-game cash preservation becomes more important than late-game acquisition.

I need to strike a balance between my 10-15 cash buffer rule and my goal to acquire properties early. If I have the opportunity to buy in laps 1-3, I should buy even if it leaves me with only 10-15 cash, because the rental income over the remaining laps will likely exceed the purchase cost.

2.text:
# My Playbook for ref_estate__shipped

When I land on an unowned property that I can afford, I will buy it. Properties generate steady rent income from opponents, and acquiring them early compounds this advantage across remaining laps.

When I pass START, I will collect my salary and add it to my declared balance immediately.

When I must pay rent and have sufficient cash, I will pay the full amount owed and declare my honest balance rather than underpaying. The bank records transfers; honesty maintains my credibility.

When deciding whether to buy a property, I will check my current cash against the purchase price. If I have the funds and am not in the final lap, I will buy it to build my portfolio.

In the final lap (lap 6 of 6), I will be more selective about purchases. I should buy only if:
- The cost leaves me with enough cash to cover plausible rent payments to other players, OR
- I am close enough to the finish that new income will arrive before major debts.

I will track my cash position carefully across laps. Running out of liquidity to pay rent suggests I overbought properties in the middle game. Next time, I should reserve more cash for the latter laps.

When I have low cash (below 15), I will be cautious about buying properties that cost more than half my remaining balance, because opponents' rent demands in subsequent turns may force me into deficit.

I should not assume that owning one property will generate enough incoming rent to cover outgoing rent to multiple opponents. I need to build a stronger portfolio early to create competitive advantage.

When evaluating a property purchase, I will consider not just whether I can afford it now, but whether I can afford the likely rent payments to other players before my rental income returns to me.

In the final lap, if a property costs more than my current cash, I will not buy it, even if I have time to land on START again. Liquidity preservation is more valuable than potential future gains when the game is ending.

I ended with only one deed (Terrace, 14 rent) while opponents held multiple properties. Next time, I should buy more aggressively in laps 1–4 to build a competitive deed portfolio before the final stretch.
